findings.description: AWS access key and secret key are embedded in plaintext in the instance user_data script, which is readable by anyone with EC2 describe permissions and also visible via the instance metadata service, effectively leaking long-lived credentials.
The instance does not configure metadata_options to require IMDSv2 (HttpTokens = required), leaving the legacy instance metadata service enabled and vulnerable to SSRF-based credential theft.
The EBS volume does not set encrypted = true (and it is explicitly commented out), leaving data at rest unencrypted and violating encryption-at-rest best practices.
The EBS snapshot inherits the unencrypted state of its source volume, meaning snapshot data at rest is also unencrypted and exposed if the snapshot is shared or accessed.
The security group allows inbound TCP port 22 (SSH) from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing administrative access to the entire internet.

The security group allows inbound TCP port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 with no compensating controls (e.g., no TLS termination configured), exposing the web service broadly; combined with public subnet placement this increases attack surface.
The security group allows all outbound traffic (protocol -1, all ports) to 0.0.0.0/0, providing an unrestricted data exfiltration and command-and-control channel.
map_public_ip_on_launch is set to true, causing instances launched in this subnet to automatically receive public IP addresses, increasing exposure to the internet unnecessarily.
map_public_ip_on_launch is set to true, causing instances launched in this subnet to automatically receive public IP addresses, increasing exposure to the internet unnecessarily.

findings.issue_category: missing encryption and public access controls
findings.description: The S3 bucket used to store VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration and no public access block, potentially leaving sensitive network traffic logs unencrypted at rest and susceptible to public exposure.
